title: A coconut and five coins
told: the history and tradition of Nanded, 1708

hook.say: quick question. is there a book you treat differently from all the others?
options: then this will feel familiar. listen.
then this one might surprise you. listen.

steps.line: 1708. By the river Godavari at Nanded, far in the south, Guru Gobind Singh knew his life was ending. His Sikhs gathered, wondering who would lead them next.
steps.label: from Sikh history and tradition

steps.q: Everyone expects him to name the next Guru. Who, or what, do you think he names?
o: The book of the Gurus’ hymns
steps.why: The book. The words of the Gurus themselves.

steps.line: He had the scripture brought out: the hymns of the Gurus, first gathered by Guru Arjan a century before.
Before it he placed five coins and a coconut, the old sign of handing on the Guruship. Then he bowed.
From now on, he told them, there would be no more human Gurus. Your Guru is the Granth, the book. The Guru Granth Sahib.

steps.q: While it’s read, someone waves a whisk, a chaur, over the Guru Granth Sahib. In old India, who got that honour?
steps.why: The chaur was waved over royalty. Sikhs wave it over the Guru Granth Sahib because it is their living Guru, sovereign over all.

steps.line: So it’s treated like a revered teacher: above everyone, under a canopy. At night it’s wrapped and carried to rest. At dawn it’s opened again.
steps.label: today

steps.q: The Guru Granth Sahib isn’t ordered by date. How is most of it arranged?
o: By the season of the year
steps.why: Most of its 1,430 pages are grouped into 31 raags, musical modes, because the hymns are meant to be sung. Kirtan is how many Sikhs meet the Guru each day.

steps.q: Each dawn the Guru Granth Sahib is opened at random and the first hymn is read aloud. How do Sikhs treat that hymn?
o: As a prediction of the day ahead
As the Guru’s order for the day
As a hymn chosen to fit the date
steps.why: It’s the hukamnama, the order of the day. Gurdwaras post it, and many Sikhs read the one from the Golden Temple each morning.

say: what amazes me is who’s inside. hymns by six of the gurus, and by holy poets who weren’t sikhs at all: kabir, a weaver. ravidas, from a caste many looked down on. sheikh farid, a muslim sufi.
almost all of it is poetry, meant to be sung. every morning a gurdwara opens it and reads the hymn where it opens, as the order of the day. sikhs don’t only read this guru. they listen to it.

steps.q: From the story, what changed for Sikhs when the Guru became a book?
o: They no longer needed to sing
Only scholars could reach the Guru
No one person sits in the Guru’s seat
steps.why: No family could claim the seat again. Guru Gobind Singh gave guidance to the Granth and authority to the Khalsa Panth, the community.

today.say: today, if you like, read the hukamnama, the order of the day, that the golden temple shares online each morning. many sikhs read it like a letter from the guru. read it, or just listen. your choice.
options: then let it be your letter for the day.
it’ll be there. a new one every morning.
